subject: International Law
title: 15. Diplomatic Envoys, Consuls and Other Representatives

segments.text: Diplomatic and consular law allows states to maintain official relations while protecting the performance of official functions.
Prepare appointment, functions, inviolability, privileges and immunities, persona non grata, and the distinction between diplomatic and consular functions.

Diplomatic law enables states to communicate and perform official functions through representatives. The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations 1961 is the central treaty framework. Diplomatic privileges and immunities are functional: they exist to ensure effective performance of the mission, not to create personal superiority or a general licence to disregard law.

The sending state and receiving state remain distinct actors. Appointment of the head of mission involves acceptance by the receiving state, and the receiving state may declare a diplomatic agent persona non grata under the Convention.

The diplomatic agent's personal inviolability and immunity from the receiving state's criminal jurisdiction are among the strongest protections. Civil and administrative immunity is subject to specified exceptions. Mission premises, archives and official communications also receive protection.

Immunity is procedural protection from the receiving state's jurisdiction; it does not mean the underlying conduct becomes lawful. The sending state may waive immunity, and the diplomat remains subject to the sending state's legal order.

Consular functions focus more on assistance to nationals, documentation, commercial and administrative functions. Consular immunities are generally more limited and closely tied to official acts under the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations 1963.

Representatives to international organizations and special missions may be governed by separate treaties, headquarters agreements or customary rules. They should not automatically be given the identical legal status of resident diplomats.

items.text: Diplomats represent the sending state in political relations; consuls perform mainly administrative, commercial and assistance functions. Their functions overlap in places but their legal status and immunities are not identical.

Appointment and acceptance create the formal relationship. Persona non grata allows the receiving state to require departure or termination of diplomatic functions without needing to litigate the diplomat's conduct.

Inviolability protects diplomatic agents, premises and communications within the applicable treaty framework. Immunity protects official functioning and is not a personal reward or permanent exemption from all law.
Consular immunities are generally more function-related than the broad protections usually associated with diplomatic agents.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not write that diplomats are “above the law.” Immunity limits the receiving state's jurisdiction in defined ways; it does not erase legal obligations.

items.text: Use Vienna Convention frameworks as the legal map.

segments.text: Immunities are functional protections of international relations, not personal rewards.
Diplomatic premises and agents receive strong protections under treaty law.
